source: In competition experiments in N. benthamiana leaves, NFR5 binds preferentially to SYMRK-ΔMLD, which experiences rapid turnover in N. benthamiana and in L. japonicus (Antolín-Llovera et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Upon overexpression in L. japonicus both NFR1 and NFR5 seem to interact with full-length SYMRK.
source: Our observation that upon overexpression in L. japonicus both NFR1 and NFR5 seem to interact with full-length SYMRK (Figure 4) suggests the formation of a ternary complex.

claim: A hypothetical ternary complex of NFR1, NFR5, and SYMRK has dual functionality: it signals through SYMRK to activate CCaMK and through the NFR1-NFR5 complex to trigger infection-related parallel pathways.
source: This hypothetical complex has dual functionality: it signals through SYMRK on one hand to activate CCaMK and through the NFR1-NFR5 complex on the other hand to trigger the infection-related parallel pathways discovered by Madsen et al. (2010) and Hayashi et al. (2010).
evidence: This is a speculative model based on the findings and supported by citations.

claim: It is possible that SYMRK has a dual—positive and negative—regulatory role.
source: It is possible that SYMRK has a dual—positive and negative—regulatory role: on the one hand SYMRK promotes signalling but on the other hand SYMRK-ΔMLD may be involved in preventing inappropriate signalling.
evidence: This is a speculative model about SYMRK function.

claim: A negative regulatory role of SYMRK would explain the exaggerated root hair response of symrk mutants to rhizobia.

claim: A LysM-RLK closely related to NFR5 has been implicated in AM signalling.

evidence: This is an interpretation based on the differential gene activation patterns.

claim: The SYMRK-mediated loss of signalling specificity may be explained by simultaneous complex formation of SYMRK with NFR1 and NFR5, and related LysM-RLKs that mediate recognition of signals from the AM fungus.
source: The SYMRK-mediated loss of signalling specificity may be explained by simultaneous complex formation of SYMRK with NFR1 and NFR5, and related LysM-RLKs that mediate recognition of signals from the AM fungus (Maillet et al., 2011; Op Den Camp et al., 2011), which results in the release of both negative regulatory mechanisms, or by an unbalanced stoichiometry of SYMRK and putative specific negative regulators of AM- and root nodule symbiosis signalling.
